# Edward Mcknight Kauffer Blue Plaque
## About This Blue Plaque
Edward McKnight Kauffer (1890-1954) was an influential American-born artist and graphic designer who made his mark in London during the early 20th century. Renowned for his bold, modernist style, Kauffer played a significant role in shaping the visual landscape of British advertising and design.
Kauffer initially traveled to Europe to pursue a career as a painter. However, he found his true calling in the world of commercial art, creating striking posters for clients such as London Underground and Shell. His innovative designs often incorporated elements of Cubism, Futurism, and Constructivism, setting him apart from his contemporaries.
Throughout his career, Kauffer collaborated with many notable figures, including the poet T.S. Eliot and the artist Mark Gertler. He also taught at the Royal College of Art, inspiring a new generation of designers. Kauffer lived in flats 139/141 of Swan Court on Chelsea Manor Street with his partner, the textile designer Marion Dorn (1896-1964). The Borough of Kensington and Chelsea, where they resided, has long been a hub for artists and creatives, with its vibrant cultural scene and proximity to major museums and galleries.
Kauffer’s legacy extends far beyond his commercial work. He was a key figure in the development of modern graphic design, and his influence can still be seen in the works of contemporary designers. This blue plaque serves as a testament to his enduring contributions to the world of art and design.

Title: Edward McKnight Kauffer: The Artist As Wanderer - New York Almanack
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
Early modern capitalism invented outdoor commercial advertising. Urban walls became prime spaces of communication; posters underpinned an emerging commodity culture. Modernist expression took hold of the street and Edward McKnight Kauffer stood in the forefront of developments.
As an artist, Edward represented an edgy generation. His psychological profile has been described as a “bird, forever in flight, forever searching for a place to come to rest”; as an emerging artist, in just two years, he passed through Chicago, Baltimore, Naples, Venice, Munich, and Paris, before establishing himself in London by early 1915. He spent his final years in New York.
**Trains and Boats and Planes**
As migration and disquietude+ are two sides of the same coin, it is not surprising that much of American writing touches upon mobility and associated themes. “Allons! the road is before us!” Walt Whitman wrote in “Song to the Open Road” (_Leaves of Grass_, 1856). Praising the freedom that drifting brings, the message became part of the nation’s consciousness.
Technology increased movement. Being on the road, following the “white lines of the freeway” without purpose and no direction home, was a way of finding one’s true self. Motion for the sake of motion was celebrated in fiction, song, and film. The “road” (potholes and all) is a microcosm of the United States.
By the early twentieth century ways of locomotion had cut open the country. Ease of mobility and reduced journey times captured the public’s imagination. Growing affluence made intercontinental travel possible. Luxury liners circled the seas. The first commercial passenger service across the Atlantic was inaugurated by the German airship Graf Zeppelin in October 1928, carrying twenty passengers (landing in Chicago in October 1933 to participate in the city’s centennial celebrations).
The world was moving. Tourist and hospitality agencies made use of the new poster medium to present themselves to the public. Sophisticated designs, supplying artists with new sources of income, exploited the wanderlust with images of exotic sceneries. Provoking a sense of adventure, they enticed the observer to book (organized) trips by train, ship, or plane.
**Chicago and Paris**

Born in December 1890 in Great Falls, Montana, Edward Kauffer was a restless youngster. He spent his childhood in Evansville, Indiana, leaving school early to paint scenery for the town’s Grand Opera House. As a teenager he joined a traveling theater company. By 1910 he had moved to San Francisco working for Paul Elder’s bookshop and, in the evenings, studying at the Mark Hopkins Institute of Art.
During that time he struck up a friendship with Joseph McKnight, a Professor at Utah University, who sensed the talent of the artist and offered to sponsor a journey to Europe. Gratefully accepting the opportunity, Kauffer adopted McKnight as his middle name.
Before setting off, he stopped in Chicago for six months, studied at the city’s Art Institute, and witnessed the ground-breaking Armory Show. The exhibition inspired him. Eager to experience the atmosphere of vanguard creativity, he planned a trip to Paris.
He traveled via Munich, home of the Blaue Reiter (Blue Rider). Founded in 1911 by Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc, this association of painters made a real impact on artistic developments. In 1912 the group published an Almanach der Blaue Reiter (with a woodcut cover by Kandinsky). Munich’s modernism, expressed in poster art and typography, touched him deeply.
Kauffer arrived in Paris in 1913 where he took a keen interest in the variety of styles and techniques on show, but his studies were cut short by the outbreak of war. Unwilling to return to America, he traveled to London with his wife, the pianist Grace Ehrlich.
**London Transport**
Some meetings are made in heaven. Frank Pick, publicity manager for the Underground Electric Railways Company of London (UERL), was a man with an eye for design management. A founding member of the Design and Industries Association (1915), Pick changed the face of London Transport. To Londoners, he was the “Titan of the Tube.”
Kauffer became a stalwart of Pick’s network of architects and designers as both men shared a vision of merging industry and graphic design. Edward believed that promoting anything from dry cleaning to an antacid (Rennie) deserved graphic attention. At the same time, he insisted that a designer must remain an artist and his work judged by aesthetic, not commercial, criteria.

Working for various clients, including Shell and Great Western Railway, Kauffer produced an extraordinary 140 posters for London Transport in a variety of styles, from impressionist snapshots (with a penchant for Japanese woodcuts), to expressionist, futurist, or cubist images.
In late 1921 he briefly moved back to New York, leaving Grace and his daughter behind. Following a small exhibition there, he hoped to sign up new clients. Despite positive reviews, only a few commissions followed. Hurt by the lack of interest in his native country, he returned to London.
Keeping in touch with French artistic developments, he made regular trips to Paris where, in 1923, he met textile designer Marion Dorn. That same year she moved to London. The couple lived together in Chelsea where they collaborated on interior design projects for clients such as Fortnum & Mason department store and Orient Line cruises.
**Covers, Posters & Politics**
In 1932 Edward started work for the publisher Lund Humphries who provided him with a studio and exhibition space in their Bedford Square building. His 1935 show at the gallery was a critical success and cemented his name as an innovative and multi-talented artist.
Kauffer’s modernist style appealed to Victor Gollancz who commissioned numerous jacket designs from him. As a publisher, Gollancz’s main concern was to encourage an awareness of current affairs. His Left Book Club, founded in 1936, aimed at tackling the dual threats of Nazism and Fascism.
It was inevitable that politics would interfere. Poster and propaganda were made for each other. Political posters became a primary means of asserting Nazi ideology and spreading anti-Semitism. Printed in bold type and produced in bright colors, its vicious messages were impossible to ignore.
Alarmed by developments in the 1930s, Kauffer lend his talents a range of combative causes, including the Peace Poster Service and the Cambridge Anti-War Council. He revealed his disdain for Fascism in a cover for Leonard Woolf’s _Quack Quack!_ (Hogarth Press, 1935). The title suggests the barnyard noise of Hitler’s and Mussolini’s oratory, which Edward matched with an image of the Hawaiian feathered war god Kukailimoku (“Snatcher of Land”).

With war imminent, Edward and Marion were forced to move to New York in 1940, departing on the S.S. Washington at the last minute. Having to rebuild their careers, they married in 1950 (and separated three years later).
**New York**
Opening at 10 February 1937, eighty-five of Kauffer’s posters had been on display at New York’s Museum of Modern Art (MOMA). It was presented as an “introduction” to American audiences. In the exhibition catalogue, Aldous Huxley paid homage to the artist’s contribution to modern design. On his return to the city in 1940, he received his first commissions from MOMA.
His break came in 1947 when American Airlines commissioned a series of posters in which Kauffer relied on his London experience of combining landscape painting and typography to convey a (commercial) message. Reconnecting with the scenery of the American west, the challenge fired his creative energy and confirmed his pioneering individual approach.
Having spent a quarter of a century in Europe, he remained an expatriate American citizen throughout. The resistance to settle (even in personal relationships), was the wellspring of his talent. Fleeing the Nazi onslaught, he had arrived in London as a refugee. When World War II made his foreign status untenable in Britain, he left and never returned. Restlessness lay at the heart of his creative being.
The rise of cultural modernism coincided with multiple waves of migration on the one hand, and increased mobility on the other. James Joyce or Ezra Pound identified artistic freedom with extra-territoriality. Rejecting separateness, modernism meant crossing boundaries, literally and metaphorically. Kauffer celebrated the worldliness of art.

McKnight Kauffer, 1940; Leonard Woolf, Quack, Quack! (1935); Edward McKnight Kauffer, poster for Pan-Am, 1953, created just before his death; Blue plaque erected in 2015 by English Heritage at Swan Court, Chelsea Manor Street._

Artist and designer. Born in Great Falls, Cascade County, Montana, USA. As an art student, he was sponsored by Professor Joseph McKnight, from whom he adopted his middle name. He moved to Paris where he met and subsequently married the textile designer Marion Dorn. At the outbreak of World War I, they moved to London. Early modern capitalism invented outdoor commercial advertising. Urban walls became prime spaces of communication; posters underpinned an emerging commodity culture. Modernist expression took hold of the street and Edward McKnight Kauffer stood in the forefront of developments.
As an artist, Edward represented an edgy generation. His psychological profile has been described as a “bird, forever in flight, forever searching for a place to come to rest”; as an emerging artist, in just two years, he passed through Chicago, Baltimore, Naples, Venice, Munich, and Paris, before establishing himself in London by early 1915. He spent his final years in New York.
**Trains and Boats and Planes**
As migration and disquietude+ are two sides of the same coin, it is not surprising that much of American writing touches upon mobility and associated themes. “Allons! the road is before us!” Walt Whitman wrote in “Song to the Open Road” (_Leaves of Grass_, 1856). Praising the freedom that drifting brings, the message became part of the nation’s consciousness.
Technology increased movement. Being on the road, following the “white lines of the freeway” without purpose and no direction home, was a way of finding one’s true self. Motion for the sake of motion was celebrated in fiction, song, and film. The “road” (potholes and all) is a microcosm of the United States.
By the early twentieth century ways of locomotion had cut open the country. Ease of mobility and reduced journey times captured the public’s imagination. Growing affluence made intercontinental travel possible. Luxury liners circled the seas. The first commercial passenger service across the Atlantic was inaugurated by the German airship Graf Zeppelin in October 1928, carrying twenty passengers (landing in Chicago in October 1933 to participate in the city’s centennial celebrations).
The world was moving. Tourist and hospitality agencies made use of the new poster medium to present themselves to the public. Sophisticated designs, supplying artists with new sources of income, exploited the wanderlust with images of exotic sceneries. Provoking a sense of adventure, they enticed the observer to book (organized) trips by train, ship, or plane.
**Chicago and Paris**

**Edward McKnight Kauffer** (14 December 1890 – 22 October 1954)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-grove-1) was an American artist and graphic designer who lived for much of his life in the United Kingdom. He worked mainly in poster art, but was also active as a painter, book illustrator and theatre designer.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-grove-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-comp-2)
texts.1:
## Early life and education
[edit]
Portrait by Carl Van Vechten, 1937
Edward Leland Kauffer was born on 14 December 1890, in Great Falls, Montana.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-CH-3) By 1910 he had moved to San Francisco working as a bookseller and studying art at the California School of Design from 1910 to 1912.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-dm-4) At around this time Professor Joseph McKnight of the University of Utah became aware of Kauffer's work, sponsored him and paid to send him to Paris for further study. In gratitude Kauffer took his sponsor's name as a middle name.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-5)
On his way to Paris, Kauffer stopped in Chicago for six months in 1912/1913 and studied at the Art Institute of Chicago. While there he witnessed the Armory Show, one of the first major exhibitions to introduce the styles of modernism to American viewers. This likely had a major impact on Kauffer, who would work in many of the same styles throughout his career. He arrived in Paris in 1913 and studied at the _Académie Moderne_ until 1914.
texts.2:
## Early life and education
At the outbreak of the First World War in 1914, he moved from Paris to London with his new wife, American pianist Grace (_née_ Ehrlich).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-mcbc-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-8) Their daughter, Ann (6 October 1920 - 1996)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-posters-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-10) would join the [Women’s Auxiliary Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Auxiliary_Air_Force "Women's Auxiliary Air Force") in the Second World War and work in photo intelligence alongside Constance Babington Smith, Eve Holiday, and Sarah Oliver, (Winston Churchill's daughter).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-11)
On a visit to Paris in 1923, he met the American textile designer Marion Dorn (1896–1964). He left his wife and daughter and subsequently lived with her in London from late 1923.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-12)
Blue plaque erected in 2015 by English Heritage at Swan Court, Chelsea Manor Street, Chelsea, London SW3 5RY, Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea.
texts.3:
## Early life and education
Kauffer remained in London for most of his career. He was briefly associated with Robert Bevan's Cumberland Market Group and had a one-man show at the Omega Workshops.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-Shone-13) In Brighton on the south coast, he designed a "novel" mural for the lobby of Embassy Court, a Modernist block of flats designed by Wells Coates in 1935. The mural consisted of "monochrome photographs ... printed directly on to a light-sensitive cellulose coating".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-Antram110-14)
Kauffer may be best known for the 140 posters that he produced for London Underground, and later London Transport. The posters span many styles: many show abstract influences, including futurism, cubism, and vorticism; others evoke impressionist influences such as Japanese woodcuts.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-16)
He created posters for Shell Oil, the Great Western Railway and other commercial clients, and also illustrated books and book covers. Later he also became interested in textiles,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-17)interior design and theatrical design.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-18) He designed the cover of the Radio Times' 1926 and 1927 Christmas Numbers.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-19) In 1930 he created a series of airbrush illustrations for _The World in 2030_ by Lord Birkenhead.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-21)

# Edward Mcknight Kauffer Blue Plaque
## About This Blue Plaque
Edward McKnight Kauffer (1890-1954) was an influential American-born artist and graphic designer who made his mark in London during the early 20th century. Renowned for his bold, modernist style, Kauffer played a significant role in shaping the visual landscape of British advertising and design.
Kauffer initially traveled to Europe to pursue a career as a painter. However, he found his true calling in the world of commercial art, creating striking posters for clients such as London Underground and Shell. His innovative designs often incorporated elements of Cubism, Futurism, and Constructivism, setting him apart from his contemporaries.
Throughout his career, Kauffer collaborated with many notable figures, including the poet T.S. Eliot and the artist Mark Gertler. He also taught at the Royal College of Art, inspiring a new generation of designers. Kauffer lived in flats 139/141 of Swan Court on Chelsea Manor Street with his partner, the textile designer Marion Dorn (1896-1964). The Borough of Kensington and Chelsea, where they resided, has long been a hub for artists and creatives, with its vibrant cultural scene and proximity to major museums and galleries.
Kauffer’s legacy extends far beyond his commercial work. He was a key figure in the development of modern graphic design, and his influence can still be seen in the works of contemporary designers. This blue plaque serves as a testament to his enduring contributions to the world of art and design.

## Edward McKnight Kauffer
Categories: Art
Countries: France, USA
Image source: uk.pinterest.com
Artist and designer. Born in Great Falls, Cascade County, Montana, USA. As an art student, he was sponsored by Professor Joseph McKnight, from whom he adopted his middle name. He moved to Paris where he met and subsequently married the textile designer Marion Dorn. At the outbreak of World War I, they moved to London. Here he made his name designing posters for the London Underground. In 1940 they moved to New York City where he produced posters, for American Airlines primarily, until his death.
Credit for this entry to: Alan Patient of www.plaquesoflondon.co.uk

Title: Edward McKnight Kauffer: The Artist As Wanderer - New York Almanack
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
Early modern capitalism invented outdoor commercial advertising. Urban walls became prime spaces of communication; posters underpinned an emerging commodity culture. Modernist expression took hold of the street and Edward McKnight Kauffer stood in the forefront of developments.
As an artist, Edward represented an edgy generation. His psychological profile has been described as a “bird, forever in flight, forever searching for a place to come to rest”; as an emerging artist, in just two years, he passed through Chicago, Baltimore, Naples, Venice, Munich, and Paris, before establishing himself in London by early 1915. He spent his final years in New York.
**Trains and Boats and Planes**
As migration and disquietude+ are two sides of the same coin, it is not surprising that much of American writing touches upon mobility and associated themes. “Allons! the road is before us!” Walt Whitman wrote in “Song to the Open Road” (_Leaves of Grass_, 1856). Praising the freedom that drifting brings, the message became part of the nation’s consciousness.
Technology increased movement. Being on the road, following the “white lines of the freeway” without purpose and no direction home, was a way of finding one’s true self. Motion for the sake of motion was celebrated in fiction, song, and film. The “road” (potholes and all) is a microcosm of the United States.
By the early twentieth century ways of locomotion had cut open the country. Ease of mobility and reduced journey times captured the public’s imagination. Growing affluence made intercontinental travel possible. Luxury liners circled the seas. The first commercial passenger service across the Atlantic was inaugurated by the German airship Graf Zeppelin in October 1928, carrying twenty passengers (landing in Chicago in October 1933 to participate in the city’s centennial celebrations).
The world was moving. Tourist and hospitality agencies made use of the new poster medium to present themselves to the public. Sophisticated designs, supplying artists with new sources of income, exploited the wanderlust with images of exotic sceneries. Provoking a sense of adventure, they enticed the observer to book (organized) trips by train, ship, or plane.
**Chicago and Paris**

Born in December 1890 in Great Falls, Montana, Edward Kauffer was a restless youngster. He spent his childhood in Evansville, Indiana, leaving school early to paint scenery for the town’s Grand Opera House. As a teenager he joined a traveling theater company. By 1910 he had moved to San Francisco working for Paul Elder’s bookshop and, in the evenings, studying at the Mark Hopkins Institute of Art.
During that time he struck up a friendship with Joseph McKnight, a Professor at Utah University, who sensed the talent of the artist and offered to sponsor a journey to Europe. Gratefully accepting the opportunity, Kauffer adopted McKnight as his middle name.
Before setting off, he stopped in Chicago for six months, studied at the city’s Art Institute, and witnessed the ground-breaking Armory Show. The exhibition inspired him. Eager to experience the atmosphere of vanguard creativity, he planned a trip to Paris.
He traveled via Munich, home of the Blaue Reiter (Blue Rider). Founded in 1911 by Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc, this association of painters made a real impact on artistic developments. In 1912 the group published an Almanach der Blaue Reiter (with a woodcut cover by Kandinsky). Munich’s modernism, expressed in poster art and typography, touched him deeply.
Kauffer arrived in Paris in 1913 where he took a keen interest in the variety of styles and techniques on show, but his studies were cut short by the outbreak of war. Unwilling to return to America, he traveled to London with his wife, the pianist Grace Ehrlich.
**London Transport**
Some meetings are made in heaven. Frank Pick, publicity manager for the Underground Electric Railways Company of London (UERL), was a man with an eye for design management. A founding member of the Design and Industries Association (1915), Pick changed the face of London Transport. To Londoners, he was the “Titan of the Tube.”
Kauffer became a stalwart of Pick’s network of architects and designers as both men shared a vision of merging industry and graphic design. Edward believed that promoting anything from dry cleaning to an antacid (Rennie) deserved graphic attention. At the same time, he insisted that a designer must remain an artist and his work judged by aesthetic, not commercial, criteria.

Working for various clients, including Shell and Great Western Railway, Kauffer produced an extraordinary 140 posters for London Transport in a variety of styles, from impressionist snapshots (with a penchant for Japanese woodcuts), to expressionist, futurist, or cubist images.
In late 1921 he briefly moved back to New York, leaving Grace and his daughter behind. Following a small exhibition there, he hoped to sign up new clients. Despite positive reviews, only a few commissions followed. Hurt by the lack of interest in his native country, he returned to London.
Keeping in touch with French artistic developments, he made regular trips to Paris where, in 1923, he met textile designer Marion Dorn. That same year she moved to London. The couple lived together in Chelsea where they collaborated on interior design projects for clients such as Fortnum & Mason department store and Orient Line cruises.
**Covers, Posters & Politics**
In 1932 Edward started work for the publisher Lund Humphries who provided him with a studio and exhibition space in their Bedford Square building. His 1935 show at the gallery was a critical success and cemented his name as an innovative and multi-talented artist.
Kauffer’s modernist style appealed to Victor Gollancz who commissioned numerous jacket designs from him. As a publisher, Gollancz’s main concern was to encourage an awareness of current affairs. His Left Book Club, founded in 1936, aimed at tackling the dual threats of Nazism and Fascism.
It was inevitable that politics would interfere. Poster and propaganda were made for each other. Political posters became a primary means of asserting Nazi ideology and spreading anti-Semitism. Printed in bold type and produced in bright colors, its vicious messages were impossible to ignore.
Alarmed by developments in the 1930s, Kauffer lend his talents a range of combative causes, including the Peace Poster Service and the Cambridge Anti-War Council. He revealed his disdain for Fascism in a cover for Leonard Woolf’s _Quack Quack!_ (Hogarth Press, 1935). The title suggests the barnyard noise of Hitler’s and Mussolini’s oratory, which Edward matched with an image of the Hawaiian feathered war god Kukailimoku (“Snatcher of Land”).

With war imminent, Edward and Marion were forced to move to New York in 1940, departing on the S.S. Washington at the last minute. Having to rebuild their careers, they married in 1950 (and separated three years later).
**New York**
Opening at 10 February 1937, eighty-five of Kauffer’s posters had been on display at New York’s Museum of Modern Art (MOMA). It was presented as an “introduction” to American audiences. In the exhibition catalogue, Aldous Huxley paid homage to the artist’s contribution to modern design. On his return to the city in 1940, he received his first commissions from MOMA.
His break came in 1947 when American Airlines commissioned a series of posters in which Kauffer relied on his London experience of combining landscape painting and typography to convey a (commercial) message. Reconnecting with the scenery of the American west, the challenge fired his creative energy and confirmed his pioneering individual approach.
Having spent a quarter of a century in Europe, he remained an expatriate American citizen throughout. The resistance to settle (even in personal relationships), was the wellspring of his talent. Fleeing the Nazi onslaught, he had arrived in London as a refugee. When World War II made his foreign status untenable in Britain, he left and never returned. Restlessness lay at the heart of his creative being.
The rise of cultural modernism coincided with multiple waves of migration on the one hand, and increased mobility on the other. James Joyce or Ezra Pound identified artistic freedom with extra-territoriality. Rejecting separateness, modernism meant crossing boundaries, literally and metaphorically. Kauffer celebrated the worldliness of art.

(Museum of Modern Art); Edward McKnight Kauffer, Fashions in Flight (1946), lithograph published by American Airlines (Smithsonian Institution); Book cover by E. (1935); Edward McKnight Kauffer, poster for Pan-Am, 1953, created just before his death; Blue plaque erected in 2015 by English Heritage at Swan Court, Chelsea Manor Street._

**Edward McKnight Kauffer** (14 December 1890 – 22 October 1954)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-grove-1) was an American artist and graphic designer who lived for much of his life in the United Kingdom. He worked mainly in poster art, but was also active as a painter, book illustrator and theatre designer.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-grove-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-comp-2)

## Early life and education
[edit]
Portrait by Carl Van Vechten, 1937
Edward Leland Kauffer was born on 14 December 1890, in Great Falls, Montana.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-CH-3) By 1910 he had moved to San Francisco working as a bookseller and studying art at the California School of Design from 1910 to 1912.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-dm-4) At around this time Professor Joseph McKnight of the University of Utah became aware of Kauffer's work, sponsored him and paid to send him to Paris for further study. In gratitude Kauffer took his sponsor's name as a middle name.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-5)
On his way to Paris, Kauffer stopped in Chicago for six months in 1912/1913 and studied at the Art Institute of Chicago. While there he witnessed the Armory Show, one of the first major exhibitions to introduce the styles of modernism to American viewers. This likely had a major impact on Kauffer, who would work in many of the same styles throughout his career. He arrived in Paris in 1913 and studied at the _Académie Moderne_ until 1914.

## Early life and education
At the outbreak of the First World War in 1914, he moved from Paris to London with his new wife, American pianist Grace (_née_ Ehrlich).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-mcbc-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-8) Their daughter, Ann (6 October 1920 - 1996)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-posters-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-10) would join the [Women’s Auxiliary Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Auxiliary_Air_Force "Women's Auxiliary Air Force") in the Second World War and work in photo intelligence alongside Constance Babington Smith, Eve Holiday, and Sarah Oliver, (Winston Churchill's daughter).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-11)
On a visit to Paris in 1923, he met the American textile designer Marion Dorn (1896–1964). He left his wife and daughter and subsequently lived with her in London from late 1923.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-12)
Blue plaque erected in 2015 by English Heritage at Swan Court, Chelsea Manor Street, Chelsea, London SW3 5RY, Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea.

## Early life and education
Kauffer remained in London for most of his career. He was briefly associated with Robert Bevan's Cumberland Market Group and had a one-man show at the Omega Workshops.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-Shone-13) In Brighton on the south coast, he designed a "novel" mural for the lobby of Embassy Court, a Modernist block of flats designed by Wells Coates in 1935. The mural consisted of "monochrome photographs ... printed directly on to a light-sensitive cellulose coating".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-Antram110-14)
Kauffer may be best known for the 140 posters that he produced for London Underground, and later London Transport. The posters span many styles: many show abstract influences, including futurism, cubism, and vorticism; others evoke impressionist influences such as Japanese woodcuts.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-16)
He created posters for Shell Oil, the Great Western Railway and other commercial clients, and also illustrated books and book covers. Later he also became interested in textiles,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-17)interior design and theatrical design.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-18) He designed the cover of the Radio Times' 1926 and 1927 Christmas Numbers.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-19) In 1930 he created a series of airbrush illustrations for _The World in 2030_ by Lord Birkenhead.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer#cite_note-21)

# Edward Mcknight Kauffer Blue Plaque
## About This Blue Plaque
Edward McKnight Kauffer (1890-1954) was an influential American-born artist and graphic designer who made his mark in London during the early 20th century. Renowned for his bold, modernist style, Kauffer played a significant role in shaping the visual landscape of British advertising and design.
Kauffer initially traveled to Europe to pursue a career as a painter. However, he found his true calling in the world of commercial art, creating striking posters for clients such as London Underground and Shell. His innovative designs often incorporated elements of Cubism, Futurism, and Constructivism, setting him apart from his contemporaries.
Throughout his career, Kauffer collaborated with many notable figures, including the poet T.S. Eliot and the artist Mark Gertler. He also taught at the Royal College of Art, inspiring a new generation of designers. Kauffer lived in flats 139/141 of Swan Court on Chelsea Manor Street with his partner, the textile designer Marion Dorn (1896-1964). The Borough of Kensington and Chelsea, where they resided, has long been a hub for artists and creatives, with its vibrant cultural scene and proximity to major museums and galleries.
Kauffer’s legacy extends far beyond his commercial work. He was a key figure in the development of modern graphic design, and his influence can still be seen in the works of contemporary designers. This blue plaque serves as a testament to his enduring contributions to the world of art and design.

Title: William Roberts: Chronology
Chunks: 9,10,11,12
William and John Roberts at Clouds Hill in the early 1930s  
1931 Another solo exhibition (sponsored by the London Artists' Association) at the Cooling Galleries – 'Recent Paintings and Drawings by William Roberts'.  
Wilfrid Evill, a solicitor and collector of modern British art, buys _The Restaurant_ from the Cooling Galleries exhibition, going on to becoming a keen collector of Roberts's work over the next 30 years.  
1932 Shows work in the Venice Biennale.  
1933?The Robertses spend two–three weeks in a flat in Alicante, Spain, owned by the brother of family friend Agustín de Irízar, lecturer in Spanish at Leeds University. (Later, Roberts and Sarah attended several guitar festivals in that country but, according to John David Roberts in the 1993 Gillian Jason Gallery catalogue, 'He did not like Spain.')  
Early 1934 The London Artists' Association is disbanded. Roberts transfers to the Lefevre Gallery, King Street, SW1.  
1934–5 _The Chess Players_ 1929–30 sparks controversy when shown as part of an exhibition of a 'Loan Collection of Contemporary British Art', organised by the Empire Art Loan Collections Society at various venues in New Zealand and Australia.The catalogue of the 'Loan Collection of Contemporary British Art' that toured New Zealand and Australia in 1934–5  
1935 Moves to 6 Provost Road, NW3.  
February–March: Exhibition at the Lefevre Gallery – 'New Paintings and Drawings by William Roberts'.  
1936 22 December: At Sotheby's, sells 35 letters from T.E. Lawrence, who had died in May 1935.  
1938 March: Exhibition at the Lefevre Gallery – 'Paintings and Drawings by William Roberts'.  

1939 Shortly after the start of the Second World War on 3 September, leaves London, staying briefly at Lonacre, Beech Tree Road, Amersham; Flint Cottage Earl Howe Road, Holmer Green, near High Wycombe; 21 St Mary's Road, Headington, Oxford; and 40 Park Town, Oxford, before moving to 76 Copse Lane, Marston, Oxford, by early June 1940, remaining there until 1946 and teaching one day a week at the Oxford Technical School. He continues to teach at the Central School in London for a couple of days a week until spring (?) 1940.76 Copse Lane, Marston – the right-hand first-floor maisonette – in 2018. The property was built in 1935, and had two bedrooms and a sitting-room, kitchen, bathroom and garden.  
12 September: From Flint Cottage, Holmer Green, writes to 'Shearman' (Harold Shearman, of the Workers' Educational Association?) for advice on getting 'some pictorial propaganda work to do'.  
16 December: Commissioned by the War Artists' Advisory Committee (WAAC) to produce six portrait drawings, for 10 guineas each.  
1940 February: To the great annoyance of the WAAC, aborts a planned trip to France to produce one of his commissioned portraits, citing travel difficulties. The number of portraits he is to draw is reduced to four.  
May: Completes the last of his commissioned portraits.  
June: After reporting that more war-artist work has been commissioned from WR, the _Liverpool Daily Post_ of 20 June comments that 'He has another distinction. He has made a habit of paying his income-tax the day after receiving the demand note. This has been done, not from any ostentation, but because, with an artist's detachment, he believed that this was the usual and expected course. He had supposed that a note accompanying the receipt and congratulating him on his public spirit was also the usual thing.'  
1940–42 Collaborates with his son on the publication of two illustrated books of verse: _Fantasy for Flute_ and _Four Fables_ (published as by David Roberts).The cover of _Fantasy for Flute_, by [John] David Roberts  

1941 January: _Munitions Factory_, commissioned by the War Artists' Advisory Committee, is included in the British Institute for Adult Education's first exhibition of war art for smaller provincial centres, which visits 24 venues between now and August 1943 and is seen by _c_.112,000 people.  
August: The War Artists' Advisory Committee rejects an offered unknown picture (probably _Demolition Squad_) and suggested topics of Indian troops and a prisoner-of-war camp, but commissions three pictures on transport-related subjects for Â£25 each.  
November: _The Control Room, Civil Defence Headquarters_, also commissioned by the WAAC, is included in the British Institute for Adult Education's second exhibition of war art for smaller provincial centres, which also visits 24 venues between now and August 1943 and is seen by over 7,000 people.  
1942 July–August: Exhibition at the Redfern Gallery, Cork Street, W1 – 'William Roberts'.  
1945 October–November: Watercolour exhibition at the Leicester Galleries, Leicester Square, WC2 – 'Drawings in Colour by William Roberts'.  
1945?Ernest Cooper, the owner of a number of health-food shops, starts buying WR's work and becomes his principal patron, eventually owning 20 oils and 49 other works, mainly watercolours.  
1946 Moves to rented rooms at 14 St Mark's Crescent, backing on to the canal near Regent's Park, NW1.14 St Mark's Crescent – Roberts's studio was the room to the right of the front door. The blue plaque commemorating his living there was unveiled in 2003 (see below). The colour scheme is as towards the end of the Robertses' time; the burglar alarm and the planting are not.  
1948 Begins exhibiting at the Royal Academy Summer Exhibition (subsequently shows there every year until his death).  
1949 November: Exhibition at the Leicester Galleries, WC2 – 'New Drawings, Satirical and Otherwise by William Roberts'.  
1950 12 February: Bernard Meninsky, Roberts's friend and colleague at the Central School, dies._(L to R)_ William Roberts, Sarah Roberts, Bernard Meninsky and an unknown woman, mid-1920s  

1951 The London Transport Board commissions a poster – _London's Fairs_ – advertising fairs accessible by public transport.  
As sole remaining sitting tenants of 14 St Mark's Crescent, the Robertses buy the house, with the help of Sarah's friend Victoria Kingsley. William, Sarah and – except for a few brief periods – John will live there for the rest of their lives.  
1956 Publishes _The Resurrection of Vorticism and the Apotheosis of Wyndham Lewis at the Tate_ – the first of five 'Vortex Pamphlets' – in response to the exhibition 'Wyndham Lewis and Vorticism' at the Tate Gallery, London, which appears to present Vorticism as the creation of Lewis alone, with Roberts and other artists as mere disciples. (Subsequent Vortex Pamphlets appear later in 1956, in 1957 and in 1958.)The catalogue for the Tate's exhibition 'Wyndham Lewis and Vorticism', which prompted Roberts's series of Vortex Pamphlets  
1956 September: Publication of _Modern English Painters_, vol. 2: _Wyndham Lewis to Henry Moore_ by Sir John Rothenstein, director of the Tate Gallery. The chapter on Roberts prompts his fourth Vortex Pamphlet, _A Reply to My Biographer Sir John Rothenstein_ (February 1957), in which he complains of errors and misrepresentations and also airs earlier grievances against the author.  
1957 21 March: _The Listener_ publishes his reminiscences of Wyndham Lewis, who had died on the 7th.  
19 August: David Bomberg, Roberts's friend from the Slade, dies.  
Publishes _Some Early Abstract and Cubist Work 1913–1920__._  
1958 February: Exhibition at the Leicester Galleries, WC2 – 'Paintings and Drawings by William Roberts'.  
25 April: Elected an Associate of the Royal Academy.

texts.9:
William and John Roberts at Clouds Hill in the early 1930s  
1931 Another solo exhibition (sponsored by the London Artists' Association) at the Cooling Galleries – 'Recent Paintings and Drawings by William Roberts'.  
Wilfrid Evill, a solicitor and collector of modern British art, buys _The Restaurant_ from the Cooling Galleries exhibition, going on to becoming a keen collector of Roberts's work over the next 30 years.  
1932 Shows work in the Venice Biennale.  
1933?The Robertses spend two–three weeks in a flat in Alicante, Spain, owned by the brother of family friend Agustín de Irízar, lecturer in Spanish at Leeds University. (Later, Roberts and Sarah attended several guitar festivals in that country but, according to John David Roberts in the 1993 Gillian Jason Gallery catalogue, 'He did not like Spain.')  
Early 1934 The London Artists' Association is disbanded. Roberts transfers to the Lefevre Gallery, King Street, SW1.  
1934–5 _The Chess Players_ 1929–30 sparks controversy when shown as part of an exhibition of a 'Loan Collection of Contemporary British Art', organised by the Empire Art Loan Collections Society at various venues in New Zealand and Australia.The catalogue of the 'Loan Collection of Contemporary British Art' that toured New Zealand and Australia in 1934–5  
1935 Moves to 6 Provost Road, NW3.  
February–March: Exhibition at the Lefevre Gallery – 'New Paintings and Drawings by William Roberts'.  
1936 22 December: At Sotheby's, sells 35 letters from T.E. Lawrence, who had died in May 1935.  
1938 March: Exhibition at the Lefevre Gallery – 'Paintings and Drawings by William Roberts'.
texts.10:
1939 Shortly after the start of the Second World War on 3 September, leaves London, staying briefly at Lonacre, Beech Tree Road, Amersham; Flint Cottage Earl Howe Road, Holmer Green, near High Wycombe; 21 St Mary's Road, Headington, Oxford; and 40 Park Town, Oxford, before moving to 76 Copse Lane, Marston, Oxford, by early June 1940, remaining there until 1946 and teaching one day a week at the Oxford Technical School. He continues to teach at the Central School in London for a couple of days a week until spring (?) 1940.76 Copse Lane, Marston – the right-hand first-floor maisonette – in 2018. The property was built in 1935, and had two bedrooms and a sitting-room, kitchen, bathroom and garden.  
12 September: From Flint Cottage, Holmer Green, writes to 'Shearman' (Harold Shearman, of the Workers' Educational Association?) for advice on getting 'some pictorial propaganda work to do'.  
16 December: Commissioned by the War Artists' Advisory Committee (WAAC) to produce six portrait drawings, for 10 guineas each.  
1940 February: To the great annoyance of the WAAC, aborts a planned trip to France to produce one of his commissioned portraits, citing travel difficulties. The number of portraits he is to draw is reduced to four.  
May: Completes the last of his commissioned portraits.  
June: After reporting that more war-artist work has been commissioned from WR, the _Liverpool Daily Post_ of 20 June comments that 'He has another distinction. He has made a habit of paying his income-tax the day after receiving the demand note. This has been done, not from any ostentation, but because, with an artist's detachment, he believed that this was the usual and expected course. He had supposed that a note accompanying the receipt and congratulating him on his public spirit was also the usual thing.'  
1940–42 Collaborates with his son on the publication of two illustrated books of verse: _Fantasy for Flute_ and _Four Fables_ (published as by David Roberts).The cover of _Fantasy for Flute_, by [John] David Roberts
texts.11:
1941 January: _Munitions Factory_, commissioned by the War Artists' Advisory Committee, is included in the British Institute for Adult Education's first exhibition of war art for smaller provincial centres, which visits 24 venues between now and August 1943 and is seen by _c_.112,000 people.  
August: The War Artists' Advisory Committee rejects an offered unknown picture (probably _Demolition Squad_) and suggested topics of Indian troops and a prisoner-of-war camp, but commissions three pictures on transport-related subjects for Â£25 each.  
November: _The Control Room, Civil Defence Headquarters_, also commissioned by the WAAC, is included in the British Institute for Adult Education's second exhibition of war art for smaller provincial centres, which also visits 24 venues between now and August 1943 and is seen by over 7,000 people.  
1942 July–August: Exhibition at the Redfern Gallery, Cork Street, W1 – 'William Roberts'.  
1945 October–November: Watercolour exhibition at the Leicester Galleries, Leicester Square, WC2 – 'Drawings in Colour by William Roberts'.  
1945?Ernest Cooper, the owner of a number of health-food shops, starts buying WR's work and becomes his principal patron, eventually owning 20 oils and 49 other works, mainly watercolours.  
1946 Moves to rented rooms at 14 St Mark's Crescent, backing on to the canal near Regent's Park, NW1.14 St Mark's Crescent – Roberts's studio was the room to the right of the front door. The blue plaque commemorating his living there was unveiled in 2003 (see below). The colour scheme is as towards the end of the Robertses' time; the burglar alarm and the planting are not.  
1948 Begins exhibiting at the Royal Academy Summer Exhibition (subsequently shows there every year until his death).  
1949 November: Exhibition at the Leicester Galleries, WC2 – 'New Drawings, Satirical and Otherwise by William Roberts'.  
1950 12 February: Bernard Meninsky, Roberts's friend and colleague at the Central School, dies._(L to R)_ William Roberts, Sarah Roberts, Bernard Meninsky and an unknown woman, mid-1920s
texts.12:
1951 The London Transport Board commissions a poster – _London's Fairs_ – advertising fairs accessible by public transport.  
As sole remaining sitting tenants of 14 St Mark's Crescent, the Robertses buy the house, with the help of Sarah's friend Victoria Kingsley. William, Sarah and – except for a few brief periods – John will live there for the rest of their lives.  
1956 Publishes _The Resurrection of Vorticism and the Apotheosis of Wyndham Lewis at the Tate_ – the first of five 'Vortex Pamphlets' – in response to the exhibition 'Wyndham Lewis and Vorticism' at the Tate Gallery, London, which appears to present Vorticism as the creation of Lewis alone, with Roberts and other artists as mere disciples. (Subsequent Vortex Pamphlets appear later in 1956, in 1957 and in 1958.)The catalogue for the Tate's exhibition 'Wyndham Lewis and Vorticism', which prompted Roberts's series of Vortex Pamphlets  
1956 September: Publication of _Modern English Painters_, vol. 2: _Wyndham Lewis to Henry Moore_ by Sir John Rothenstein, director of the Tate Gallery. The chapter on Roberts prompts his fourth Vortex Pamphlet, _A Reply to My Biographer Sir John Rothenstein_ (February 1957), in which he complains of errors and misrepresentations and also airs earlier grievances against the author.  
1957 21 March: _The Listener_ publishes his reminiscences of Wyndham Lewis, who had died on the 7th.  
19 August: David Bomberg, Roberts's friend from the Slade, dies.  
Publishes _Some Early Abstract and Cubist Work 1913–1920__._  
1958 February: Exhibition at the Leicester Galleries, WC2 – 'Paintings and Drawings by William Roberts'.  
25 April: Elected an Associate of the Royal Academy.

William and John Roberts at Clouds Hill in the early 1930s  
1931 Another solo exhibition (sponsored by the London Artists' Association) at the Cooling Galleries – 'Recent Paintings and Drawings by William Roberts'.  
Wilfrid Evill, a solicitor and collector of modern British art, buys _The Restaurant_ from the Cooling Galleries exhibition, going on to becoming a keen collector of Roberts's work over the next 30 years.  
1932 Shows work in the Venice Biennale.  
1933?The Robertses spend two–three weeks in a flat in Alicante, Spain, owned by the brother of family friend Agustín de Irízar, lecturer in Spanish at Leeds University. (Later, Roberts and Sarah attended several guitar festivals in that country but, according to John David Roberts in the 1993 Gillian Jason Gallery catalogue, 'He did not like Spain.')  
Early 1934 The London Artists' Association is disbanded. Roberts transfers to the Lefevre Gallery, King Street, SW1.  
1934–5 _The Chess Players_ 1929–30 sparks controversy when shown as part of an exhibition of a 'Loan Collection of Contemporary British Art', organised by the Empire Art Loan Collections Society at various venues in New Zealand and Australia.The catalogue of the 'Loan Collection of Contemporary British Art' that toured New Zealand and Australia in 1934–5  
1935 Moves to 6 Provost Road, NW3.  
February–March: Exhibition at the Lefevre Gallery – 'New Paintings and Drawings by William Roberts'.  
1936 22 December: At Sotheby's, sells 35 letters from T.E. Lawrence, who had died in May 1935.  
1938 March: Exhibition at the Lefevre Gallery – 'Paintings and Drawings by William Roberts'.  

1939 Shortly after the start of the Second World War on 3 September, leaves London, staying briefly at Lonacre, Beech Tree Road, Amersham; Flint Cottage Earl Howe Road, Holmer Green, near High Wycombe; 21 St Mary's Road, Headington, Oxford; and 40 Park Town, Oxford, before moving to 76 Copse Lane, Marston, Oxford, by early June 1940, remaining there until 1946 and teaching one day a week at the Oxford Technical School. He continues to teach at the Central School in London for a couple of days a week until spring (?) 1940.76 Copse Lane, Marston – the right-hand first-floor maisonette – in 2018. The property was built in 1935, and had two bedrooms and a sitting-room, kitchen, bathroom and garden.  
12 September: From Flint Cottage, Holmer Green, writes to 'Shearman' (Harold Shearman, of the Workers' Educational Association?) for advice on getting 'some pictorial propaganda work to do'.  
16 December: Commissioned by the War Artists' Advisory Committee (WAAC) to produce six portrait drawings, for 10 guineas each.  
1940 February: To the great annoyance of the WAAC, aborts a planned trip to France to produce one of his commissioned portraits, citing travel difficulties. The number of portraits he is to draw is reduced to four.  
May: Completes the last of his commissioned portraits.  
June: After reporting that more war-artist work has been commissioned from WR, the _Liverpool Daily Post_ of 20 June comments that 'He has another distinction. He has made a habit of paying his income-tax the day after receiving the demand note. This has been done, not from any ostentation, but because, with an artist's detachment, he believed that this was the usual and expected course. He had supposed that a note accompanying the receipt and congratulating him on his public spirit was also the usual thing.'  
1940–42 Collaborates with his son on the publication of two illustrated books of verse: _Fantasy for Flute_ and _Four Fables_ (published as by David Roberts).The cover of _Fantasy for Flute_, by [John] David Roberts  

1941 January: _Munitions Factory_, commissioned by the War Artists' Advisory Committee, is included in the British Institute for Adult Education's first exhibition of war art for smaller provincial centres, which visits 24 venues between now and August 1943 and is seen by _c_.112,000 people.  
August: The War Artists' Advisory Committee rejects an offered unknown picture (probably _Demolition Squad_) and suggested topics of Indian troops and a prisoner-of-war camp, but commissions three pictures on transport-related subjects for Â£25 each.  
November: _The Control Room, Civil Defence Headquarters_, also commissioned by the WAAC, is included in the British Institute for Adult Education's second exhibition of war art for smaller provincial centres, which also visits 24 venues between now and August 1943 and is seen by over 7,000 people.  
1942 July–August: Exhibition at the Redfern Gallery, Cork Street, W1 – 'William Roberts'.  
1945 October–November: Watercolour exhibition at the Leicester Galleries, Leicester Square, WC2 – 'Drawings in Colour by William Roberts'.  
1945?Ernest Cooper, the owner of a number of health-food shops, starts buying WR's work and becomes his principal patron, eventually owning 20 oils and 49 other works, mainly watercolours.  
1946 Moves to rented rooms at 14 St Mark's Crescent, backing on to the canal near Regent's Park, NW1.14 St Mark's Crescent – Roberts's studio was the room to the right of the front door. The blue plaque commemorating his living there was unveiled in 2003 (see below). The colour scheme is as towards the end of the Robertses' time; the burglar alarm and the planting are not.  
1948 Begins exhibiting at the Royal Academy Summer Exhibition (subsequently shows there every year until his death).  
1949 November: Exhibition at the Leicester Galleries, WC2 – 'New Drawings, Satirical and Otherwise by William Roberts'.  
1950 12 February: Bernard Meninsky, Roberts's friend and colleague at the Central School, dies._(L to R)_ William Roberts, Sarah Roberts, Bernard Meninsky and an unknown woman, mid-1920s  

1951 The London Transport Board commissions a poster – _London's Fairs_ – advertising fairs accessible by public transport.  
As sole remaining sitting tenants of 14 St Mark's Crescent, the Robertses buy the house, with the help of Sarah's friend Victoria Kingsley. William, Sarah and – except for a few brief periods – John will live there for the rest of their lives.  
1956 Publishes _The Resurrection of Vorticism and the Apotheosis of Wyndham Lewis at the Tate_ – the first of five 'Vortex Pamphlets' – in response to the exhibition 'Wyndham Lewis and Vorticism' at the Tate Gallery, London, which appears to present Vorticism as the creation of Lewis alone, with Roberts and other artists as mere disciples. (Subsequent Vortex Pamphlets appear later in 1956, in 1957 and in 1958.)The catalogue for the Tate's exhibition 'Wyndham Lewis and Vorticism', which prompted Roberts's series of Vortex Pamphlets  
1956 September: Publication of _Modern English Painters_, vol. 2: _Wyndham Lewis to Henry Moore_ by Sir John Rothenstein, director of the Tate Gallery. The chapter on Roberts prompts his fourth Vortex Pamphlet, _A Reply to My Biographer Sir John Rothenstein_ (February 1957), in which he complains of errors and misrepresentations and also airs earlier grievances against the author.

Publishes _Some Early Abstract and Cubist Work 1913–1920__._

# ‘Plymouth Pier from the Hoe’ by Charles Ginner
The painting is by an artist called Isaac Charles Ginner (1878-1952). Born in the south of France to British parents, he settled in London in 1910 where he became associated with fellow artists Spencer Gore and Harold Gilman and a key member of the Camden Town Group.
Ginner was brilliant at painting buildings in an urban context – possibly not surprising given that he worked in an engineer’s office and an architect’s office before he moved to England.
He was passionate about representing contemporary life and ‘all it contains of great or of weak, of beautiful or of sordid’ and believed that painting ‘becomes a document for future ages’.
The pier was a hub of Plymouth life when he painted this, using flat brushes to methodically apply a thick coat of vibrant paint as he captured the energy of a moment in between two World Wars.
The pier first opened on May 29, 1884 and was heralded as ‘one of the finest structures of the kind on the coast’. It was designed by Eugenius Birch (1818-1884), an architect and civil engineer who is often described as ‘the father of the promenade pier’.
Birch was born in London and was fascinated by engineering from a young age, joining an engineering works as an apprentice before studying at the Mechanics Institute. He went on to become a Member of the Institution of Civil Engineering and establish an engineering partnership with his brother. The company worked on a wide range of projects including railways, viaducts, bridges and waterworks. He also designed Exmouth Docks and Ilfracombe Harbour.
Between 1855 and 1884, 14 piers designed by Birch were built. Five of them are still open today. They were located in Aberystwyth (Wales), Blackpool, Bournemouth, Brighton, Deal, Eastbourne, Hastings, Hornsea (Yorkshire), Lytham (Lancashire), Margate, Scarborough, Weston-super-mare, and, of course, Plymouth.
The facilities on the pier here initially included shops, a clock tower and a landing stage. In 1891, a 2,000-seat pavilion was added turning it into a venue for concerts, parties, dancing, boxing and wrestling.

The artist Spencer Gore was at the cutting edge of British art in the early 20th century. A close friend of Walter Sickert, he was a founding member of the Fitzroy Street Group, the Camden Town Group and the London Group. He is commemorated with a blue plaque at 31 Mornington Crescent, where he lived from about 1909 until 1912.
A self-portrait by Spencer Gore painted in 1914, shortly before his death from pneumonia  © National Portrait Gallery, London

# GORE, SPENCER FREDERICK (1878-1914)
## ARTISTIC DEVELOPMENT
Gore attended the Slade School of Fine Art from 1897 until 1901, where he was introduced to English impressionism by his painting tutor Philip Wilson Steer. While there he made lasting friendships with Albert Rutherston and Harold Gilman, Augustus John and Wyndham Lewis. His most important friendship, however, was to be with Walter Sickert, whom he met while on a painting trip to France in 1904.
Both men lived in London from 1905 onwards, and Sickert became an influential artistic guide and champion for Gore. Gore’s painting style responded to the broken colour and handling of the French Impressionists. He would sketch and paint, sometimes in Sickert’s studio, or in the music halls and streets of London. His subjects reflected the mix of London’s social culture portraying the streets and homes of working men and women. In the hands of Gore, Sickert wrote, dreary and hopeless scenes were ‘transformed into loveliness’.

# GORE, SPENCER FREDERICK (1878-1914)
## FROM FITZROY TO CAMDEN
In 1907 Gore helped Sickert set up the Fitzroy Street Group, an informal collection of artists who gathered on Saturday afternoons at 19 Fitzroy Street, Fitzrovia. The first members included two women, Ethel Sands and her partner Nan Hudson – plus Harold Gilman and Malcolm Drummond, with Robert Bevan and Charles Ginner joining them after 1908. Sickert defined the Group’s purpose as providing the opportunity for younger artists to show 'Little pictures for Little Patrons’ – affordable pictures at a scale that would fit homes rather than for the grander exhibition shows, and to accustom people to seeing modern and innovative works.
In 1911 Gore and Sickert set up another artists’ group: the men-only Camden Town Group. The 16 artists, who included Wyndham Lewis, Lucien Pissarro and Duncan Grant, had little stylistic bond between them, but shared the ambition to respond to modernist ideals and truthfully observe the social and cultural life of modern Britain.

# GORE, SPENCER FREDERICK (1878-1914)
## MORNINGTON CRESCENT
In 1909 Gore moved to 31 Mornington Crescent in Camden Town, where he is now commemorated with a blue plaque. The blue plaque to Sickert is also located nearby at 6 Mornington Crescent, where he lived from 1905 until about 1908, shortly before Gore’s arrival.
The three years that Gore lived here saw him progress into an artist of ability and innovation. One of his four works shown in the first Camden Town Group exhibition was Mornington Crescent, a view painted from his window across the gardens to Hampstead Road. At least eight works in total were painted here: two showing the interior of the comfortable sitting room he shared with his landlord and six documenting either views from his window, or from within the residents’ private garden. Unfortunately the view Gore painted has been lost. The private gardens are now occupied by the Carreras Cigarette Factory, the Egyptian-style façade of which faces the Hampstead Road.
In 1926 the artist Walter Bayes wrote to _The Times_ to suggest that a new row of shops about to be built in Mornington Crescent should be called ‘Spencer Gore’s Grove’. Bayes recalled Gore ‘standing at his easel in the most inclement weathers painting so many charming pictures there to the accompaniment of the hum of the trams’.
Gore moved out of number 31 in 1912 after his marriage to Mary Johanna Kerr (1889–1968), known as Mollie. The couple moved to Richmond the following year, and from there Gore worked to bring together new artists for the Camden Town Group’s successor, the London Group. Their first exhibition in 1914 was to be Gore’s swansong: he contracted influenza which turned to pneumonia, and died on 27 March, aged 35.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
_Self-portrait_
_Hartington Square_
**Spencer Frederick Gore** (26 May 1878 – 27 March 1914)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-1) was a British painter of landscapes, music-hall scenes and interiors, usually with single figures. He was the first president of the Camden Town Group,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Bonett-2) and was influenced by the Post-Impressionists.
He was born on 26 May 1878 at Epsom in Surrey, the youngest of the four children of the Wimbledon tennis champion, Spencer Gore and his wife Amy Margaret (née Smith). His father's brother was the theologian Charles Gore. His father sent him to board at Harrow School in Middlesex (now Greater London). He went on to study painting in London at the Slade School of Fine Art, where he was a contemporary of Harold Gilman.
In 1904 Albert Rutherston introduced Gore to Walter Sickert at Dieppe; and afterwards he associated in Fitzroy Street, London, with Sickert, Lucien Pissarro, Harold Gilman and Charles Ginner. In 1909 he became a member of the New English Art Club, and in 1910 contributed an article to _The Art News_ on "The Third London Salon of the Allied Artists Association".
In 1911 he was a co-founder and first president of the Camden Town Group. There is a Blue plaque at 31 Mornington Crescent where he lived and worked between 1909 and 1912.
In January 1912 he married Mary Joanna ("Molly") Kerr, with whom he had two children– Margaret Elizabeth (1912–1994) and Frederick John Pym (1913–2009); the latter would become well known as the painter Frederick Gore. His widow died at Meopham, Kent in 1968.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-3)
In 1913 he became a member of the London Group.

His later works show growing concern with pictorial construction, under the influence of the Post-Impressionists. He experimented with colour in his works, as may be seen in his painting _Hartington Square_.
Gore painted a series of thirty-two landscapes in Richmond Park during the last months of his life.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Art_UK_1-4) His painting _From a Window in Cambrian Road, Richmond_[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-5) shows the view from a top-floor window at the rear of 6 Cambrian Road, near the park's Cambrian Gate entrance, where he and his family moved to in 1913.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Cambrian_Road_window-7) This may be the last picture Gore worked on before his death.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Cambrian_Road_window-7) According to Tate curator Helena Bonett, Gore's early death from pneumonia, two months before what would have been his 36th birthday, was brought on by his painting outdoors in Richmond Park in the cold and wet winter months.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Tate_2-8)

Gore's painting _Richmond Park_, thought to have been painted in the autumn of 1913 or shortly before the artist's death in March 1914, was exhibited at the Paterson and Carfax Gallery[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Carfax-9) in 1920. In 1939 it was exhibited in Warsaw, Helsinki and Stockholm by the British Council as _Group of Trees_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Tate_1-10) It is now in the collection of the Tate Gallery under its original title but is not currently on display.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Tate_1-10) It is not certain where in the park the picture was made but a row of trees close to the pond near Cambrian Gate has a very close resemblance to those in the painting.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-11) Another Gore painting, with the same title (_Richmond Park_), painted in 1914, is at the Ashmolean Museum. His painting _Wood in Richmond Park_ is in the Birmingham Art Gallery's collection.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Wood_in_Richmond_Park-12)
Two of Gore's artworks, _Brighton Pier_ and _Richmond Houses_, appear in the first number of the landmark modernist journal, _BLAST_, published some three months after Gore's death.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-13) There features also an obituary piece by Wyndham Lewis, who edited the magazine, and who eulogises Gore's "dogged, almost romantic industry, his passion for the delicate objects set in the London atmosphere around him, his grey conception of the artist's life, his gentleness and fineness, [which] would have matured into an abundant personal art".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-14)

He died at Richmond, Surrey, on 27 March 1914, aged 35 and was buried in Hertingfordbury in Hertfordshire, where his mother lived.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-15)
Spencer Gore gave John Doman Turner artistic training from 1908 to 1913 in a series of thirty letters. The teaching was probably carried out via correspondence because Doman Turner was deaf. The letters are now held in the Gore family collection. Doman Turner was a member of the Camden Town Group, having been elected by Gore, but was shy and unsure of his abilities, which probably led him to resign his membership of the London Group soon after it was formed on 27 November 1913.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-16)

Bayes recalled Gore ‘standing at his easel in the most inclement weathers painting so many charming pictures there to the accompaniment of the hum of the trams’.
Gore moved out of number 31 in 1912 after his marriage to Mary Johanna Kerr (1889–1968), known as Mollie. The couple moved to Richmond the following year, and from there Gore worked to bring together new artists for the Camden Town Group’s successor, the London Group. Their first exhibition in 1914 was to be Gore’s swansong: he contracted influenza which turned to pneumonia, and died on 27 March, aged 35.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
_Self-portrait_
_Hartington Square_
**Spencer Frederick Gore** (26 May 1878 – 27 March 1914)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-1) was a British painter of landscapes, music-hall scenes and interiors, usually with single figures. He was the first president of the Camden Town Group,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Bonett-2) and was influenced by the Post-Impressionists.
He was born on 26 May 1878 at Epsom in Surrey, the youngest of the four children of the Wimbledon tennis champion, Spencer Gore and his wife Amy Margaret (née Smith). His father's brother was the theologian Charles Gore. His father sent him to board at Harrow School in Middlesex (now Greater London). He went on to study painting in London at the Slade School of Fine Art, where he was a contemporary of Harold Gilman.
In 1904 Albert Rutherston introduced Gore to Walter Sickert at Dieppe; and afterwards he associated in Fitzroy Street, London, with Sickert, Lucien Pissarro, Harold Gilman and Charles Ginner. In 1909 he became a member of the New English Art Club, and in 1910 contributed an article to _The Art News_ on "The Third London Salon of the Allied Artists Association".
In 1911 he was a co-founder and first president of the Camden Town Group. There is a Blue plaque at 31 Mornington Crescent where he lived and worked between 1909 and 1912.
In January 1912 he married Mary Joanna ("Molly") Kerr, with whom he had two children– Margaret Elizabeth (1912–1994) and Frederick John Pym (1913–2009); the latter would become well known as the painter Frederick Gore. His widow died at Meopham, Kent in 1968.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-3)
In 1913 he became a member of the London Group.
texts.1:
His later works show growing concern with pictorial construction, under the influence of the Post-Impressionists. He experimented with colour in his works, as may be seen in his painting _Hartington Square_.
Gore painted a series of thirty-two landscapes in Richmond Park during the last months of his life.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Art_UK_1-4) His painting _From a Window in Cambrian Road, Richmond_[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-5) shows the view from a top-floor window at the rear of 6 Cambrian Road, near the park's Cambrian Gate entrance, where he and his family moved to in 1913.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Cambrian_Road_window-7) This may be the last picture Gore worked on before his death.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Cambrian_Road_window-7) According to Tate curator Helena Bonett, Gore's early death from pneumonia, two months before what would have been his 36th birthday, was brought on by his painting outdoors in Richmond Park in the cold and wet winter months.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Tate_2-8)
texts.2:
Gore's painting _Richmond Park_, thought to have been painted in the autumn of 1913 or shortly before the artist's death in March 1914, was exhibited at the Paterson and Carfax Gallery[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Carfax-9) in 1920. In 1939 it was exhibited in Warsaw, Helsinki and Stockholm by the British Council as _Group of Trees_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Tate_1-10) It is now in the collection of the Tate Gallery under its original title but is not currently on display.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Tate_1-10) It is not certain where in the park the picture was made but a row of trees close to the pond near Cambrian Gate has a very close resemblance to those in the painting.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-11) Another Gore painting, with the same title (_Richmond Park_), painted in 1914, is at the Ashmolean Museum. His painting _Wood in Richmond Park_ is in the Birmingham Art Gallery's collection.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-Wood_in_Richmond_Park-12)
Two of Gore's artworks, _Brighton Pier_ and _Richmond Houses_, appear in the first number of the landmark modernist journal, _BLAST_, published some three months after Gore's death.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-13) There features also an obituary piece by Wyndham Lewis, who edited the magazine, and who eulogises Gore's "dogged, almost romantic industry, his passion for the delicate objects set in the London atmosphere around him, his grey conception of the artist's life, his gentleness and fineness, [which] would have matured into an abundant personal art".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-14)
texts.3:
He died at Richmond, Surrey, on 27 March 1914, aged 35 and was buried in Hertingfordbury in Hertfordshire, where his mother lived.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-15)
Spencer Gore gave John Doman Turner artistic training from 1908 to 1913 in a series of thirty letters. The teaching was probably carried out via correspondence because Doman Turner was deaf. The letters are now held in the Gore family collection. Doman Turner was a member of the Camden Town Group, having been elected by Gore, but was shy and unsure of his abilities, which probably led him to resign his membership of the London Group soon after it was formed on 27 November 1913.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist)#cite_note-16)

*   Upstone, Robert. _Modern Painters: The Camden Town Group_, exhibition catalogue, Tate Britain, London, 2008. ISBN1-85437-781-7

# ‘Plymouth Pier from the Hoe’ by Charles Ginner
The painting is by an artist called Isaac Charles Ginner (1878-1952). Born in the south of France to British parents, he settled in London in 1910 where he became associated with fellow artists Spencer Gore and Harold Gilman and a key member of the Camden Town Group.
Ginner was brilliant at painting buildings in an urban context – possibly not surprising given that he worked in an engineer’s office and an architect’s office before he moved to England.
He was passionate about representing contemporary life and ‘all it contains of great or of weak, of beautiful or of sordid’ and believed that painting ‘becomes a document for future ages’.
The pier was a hub of Plymouth life when he painted this, using flat brushes to methodically apply a thick coat of vibrant paint as he captured the energy of a moment in between two World Wars.
The pier first opened on May 29, 1884 and was heralded as ‘one of the finest structures of the kind on the coast’. It was designed by Eugenius Birch (1818-1884), an architect and civil engineer who is often described as ‘the father of the promenade pier’.
Birch was born in London and was fascinated by engineering from a young age, joining an engineering works as an apprentice before studying at the Mechanics Institute. He went on to become a Member of the Institution of Civil Engineering and establish an engineering partnership with his brother. The company worked on a wide range of projects including railways, viaducts, bridges and waterworks. He also designed Exmouth Docks and Ilfracombe Harbour.
Between 1855 and 1884, 14 piers designed by Birch were built. Five of them are still open today. They were located in Aberystwyth (Wales), Blackpool, Bournemouth, Brighton, Deal, Eastbourne, Hastings, Hornsea (Yorkshire), Lytham (Lancashire), Margate, Scarborough, Weston-super-mare, and, of course, Plymouth.
The facilities on the pier here initially included shops, a clock tower and a landing stage. In 1891, a 2,000-seat pavilion was added turning it into a venue for concerts, parties, dancing, boxing and wrestling.

# GORE, SPENCER FREDERICK (1878-1914)
Plaque erected in **2017** by **English Heritage** at **31 Mornington Crescent, London, NW1 7RE, London Borough of Camden**
All images © English Heritage
Profession
Painter
